# Mettagūmāṇavapucchā (Snp 5.5 (PTS Snp 201))

**ID:** Snp 5.5 (PTS Snp 201)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Mettagūmāṇavapucchā
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mettagūmāṇavapucchā* ("The Questions of the Student Mettagū", also translated as "Mettagū's Questions") is the fifth discourse of the *Pārāyaṇavagga* in the *Suttanipāta*, comprising verses 1049–1060 (PTS Snp 201) [Norman 1997-2001; Saddhatissa 2013; Anderson and Smith 1913]. In this dialogue, the student Mettagū asks the Buddha about the origin of the manifold sufferings in the world and how one crosses over the flood of birth, old age, sorrow, and grief [Hazra 1994; Anderson and Smith 1913]. The Buddha explains that *upadhi* (attachment or possessiveness) is the fundamental source of pain and suffering, and that wise persons who thoroughly understand the Dhamma can cross the stream of birth and aging [Hazra 1994; Schmithausen 1987]. Metrically, the majority of the verses are composed in Triṣṭubh, along with mixed Śloka and Triṣṭubh lines [Norman 1997-2001].

The text is commented upon in the canonical *Cullaniddesa*, specifically in the *Mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa* (Cnd 8) as well as the introductory *Pucchā* (Cnd 2) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus detects extensive text reuse between this discourse and various other *Niddesa* chapters—including the *Dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa* (Cnd 9), *Puṇṇakamāṇavapucchāniddesa* (Cnd 7), and *Upasīvamāṇavapucchāniddesa* (Cnd 10)—as well as with the *Dvayatānupassanāsutta* (Snp 3.12) [DharmaNexus]. Outside the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records minor machine alignments with Tibetan versions of the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Mañjuśrījñānasattvasyāparamārthanāmasaṃgīti* [DharmaNexus], while modern philosophical studies have noted conceptual parallels between verses such as Sn 1051ab and Yogācāra discussions on the origin of suffering [Schmithausen 1987].
